articles.full_text:
दिल्ली-NCR में फिर बदलेगा मौसम का मिजाज, बारिश को लेकर IMD का अलर्ट जारी
मौसम विभाग के अनुसार राजधानी दिल्ली में आज बादल छाए रहेंगे और कुछ इलाकों में हल्की से मध्यम बारिश या बौछारें पड़ सकती हैं.
नई दिल्ली: दिल्ली-NCR में आज सोमवार को मौसम का मिजाज बदला हुआ रहने वाला है. राजधानी में आज दिनभर बादल छाए रहने और कई इलाकों में बारिश होने की संभावना है. इसके साथ ही 15 सितंबर को भी बारिश का अलर्ट दिया गया है.
दिल्ली-NCR में बीते दिन यानि रविवार को ज्यादातर इलाकों में तेज धूप रही. इसके साथ दिन के समय बीच-बीच में हल्के बादलों की आवजााही भी जारी रही, लेकिन कुल मिलाकर तेज धूप के चलते तापमान में इजाफा दर्ज किया गया. दिल्ली की मानक वेधशाला सफदरजंग में दिन का अधिकतम तापमान 35.1 डिग्री सेल्सियस रिकॉर्ड किया गया जो सामान्य से 1.3 डिग्री सेल्सियस ज्यादा है. वहीं न्यूनतम तापमान 26.2 डिग्री सेल्सियस रिकॉर्ड किया गया जो सामान्य से 1.1 डिग्री सेल्सियस ज्यादा है.
आज के मौसम का हाल
मौसम विभाग के अनुसार राजधानी दिल्ली में आज आसमान में बादल छाए रहेंगे और कुछ इलाकों में हल्की से मध्यम बारिश या बौछारें पड़ सकती हैं. इस दौरान अधिकतम तापमान लगभग 31 से 33 डिग्री और न्यूनतम तापमान 25 से 26 डिग्री सेल्सियस के आसपास रहने की संभावना है. इसके साथ ही हवा में नमी का स्तर अधिक लगभग 70% से 90% के बीच रहने के कारण उमस महसूस हो सकती है, लेकिन ठंडी हवाओं से राहत भी मिलेगी.
इसके बाद 15 और 16 सितंबर को दिल्ली-NCR में छिटपुट आंशिक रूप से बादल छाए रहने और सुबह से दोपहर के बीच कुछ जगहों पर हल्की बारिश की संभावना जताई है. IMD ने 15 सितंबर को दिल्ली में अधिकतम तापमान 31 से 33 डिग्री सेल्सियस के आसपास रिकॉर्ड किए जाने की संभावना जताई है.
केंद्रीय प्रदूषण एवं नियंत्रण बोर्ड (CPCB) के अनुसार राजधानी दिल्ली में सोमवार सुबह 7 बजे तक औसतन वायु गुणवत्ता सूचकांक 77 अंक पर बना हुआ है, जबकि दिल्ली एनसीआर के शहर फरीदाबाद में 88, गुरुग्राम में 73, गाजियाबाद में 85, ग्रेटर नोएडा में 72 और नोएडा में 78 अंक पर बना हुआ है. राजधानी दिल्ली के अधिकांश इलाकों में AQI लेवल 100 से नीचे बना हुआ है। जबकि कुछ इलाकों में AQI लेवल 100 से ऊपर और 200 के बीच में बना हुआ है.

articles.full_text:
Diamondback moths exposed to repeated heat for 3 years evolved traits that helped their descendants develop faster and survive extreme temperatures better. A 2026 study titled ‘
Experimental evolution to thermal stress indicates climate resilience in a cosmopolitan arthropod’ tested moth populations under different temperatures for dozens of generations. It was carried out to examine how they responded to prolonged thermal stress. The heat-selected population eventually showed faster development, higher female fertility and stronger survival at temperatures that caused greater mortality in moths kept under favourable conditions. The researchers also identified changes in genes, metabolism and DNA regulation linked to the insects’ ability to cope with heat.
Three years of extreme heat reshaped diamondback moths
The researchers raised diamondback moths under controlled temperature conditions for three years. The heat-selected group experienced temperatures alternating between 32°C and 27°C over a 12-hour cycle. Another group was exposed to colder conditions of 15°C and 10°C, while a third group was maintained at a constant 26°C as the ancestral comparison.
The heat-selected population went through about 75 generations during the experiment.
This gave natural selection many opportunities to favour characteristics that helped the insects cope with high temperatures.
The researchers then compared the evolved populations with the ancestral strain to determine whether prolonged exposure had produced lasting differences.
Diamondback Moth - Plutella xylostella
What changed in the heat-selected moths
The heat-selected moths completed their development more quickly than the ancestral population. They also showed higher female fertility and a greater rate of population growth.
These changes could give the insects an advantage when conditions are difficult. A shorter development period allows them to reach adulthood sooner, while greater fertility can increase the number of offspring produced by a population.
How did the moths respond to extreme temperatures
The scientists exposed different life stages to temperatures higher than those during the long-term heat treatment. The heat-selected strain generally survived better than the ancestral strain at these temperatures.
At 42°C, eggs, third-stage larvae and adults from the heat-selected population showed higher survival. The difference was particularly pronounced in third-stage larvae. After 120 minutes at 42°C, survival was 26.67% in the heat-selected strain compared with 13.33% in the ancestral strain, according to the study.
Heat-selected pupae also survived better when exposed to 43°C and 44°C. These tests showed that the evolved population could withstand short periods of temperatures more severe than those used during its long-term selection.
Heat exposure changed the genetic makeup of the moths
The researchers examined gene activity, metabolism and DNA regulation to identify biological changes associated with the different temperatures.
They found major differences in gene activity and metabolic processes between various populations. Lipid metabolism was among the affected processes. As per the study, reduced lipid metabolism could help insects manage energy demands during thermal stress.
One important finding involved the PxSODC gene. It is associated with an enzyme that helps cells deal with harmful molecules produced during stress. The researchers identified a mutation in this gene in the heat-selected population and found that it improved the enzyme’s ability to remove these damaging molecules.
The study also investigated DNA methylation, a chemical process that can influence how genes function. They focused on PxDnmt1, a gene involved in maintaining DNA methylation. When its activity was reduced, the moths showed changes in their responses to thermal stress.
Female moths with reduced PxDnmt1 activity became less able to withstand very high temperatures, while pupae became more sensitive to cold. This suggested that changes in how their genes were controlled also helped the moths adjust to temperature stress.
What does the study reveal about the moth’s future
The study provides evidence that diamondback moth populations can respond rapidly to sustained high temperatures. Within three years of experimental evolution, the heat-selected population had developed differences in development, reproduction and tolerance to extreme heat.
Because diamondback moths are important agricultural pests, such changes could have wider implications. The scientists note that thermal adaptation may affect predictions about where the species can survive and reproduce as temperatures change.
However, the experiment was conducted under controlled lab conditions. Natural populations encounter many additional pressures like changing weather, food availability and other environmental factors.
But still, the study demonstrates how quickly a species with short generations can respond when the same environmental pressure persists over many generations.

Belgian Fries Under Threat as Extreme Heat Shrinks Potato Crop
Belgium’s famous fries could face a supply squeeze after extreme weather left this year’s potato crop unusually small, raising concerns over tighter supplies and potentially higher prices for processors, fry shops and consumers.
Belgian potato farmers are reporting severe problems in the fields as exceptionally hot and dry summer conditions have prevented potatoes from developing to their normal size. The situation is particularly concerning for the country’s processing industry, which relies heavily on large, elongated potatoes suitable for producing frozen fries.
Potatoes Too Small for Fries
In Amay, near the eastern Belgian city of Liège, farmer Mathieu Comijn is harvesting Bintje potatoes from extremely dry soil. Some potatoes are barely the size of ping-pong balls, far below the size normally required for efficient fry production.
Mathieu Comijn, Belgian potato farmer:
"You can see the soil is extremely dry. Normally, they should be at least four times this size. At the moment we can't make fries with these potatoes."
The difficult growing conditions followed a challenging spring. Heavy rain and storms at the end of spring weakened the soil, while exceptionally hot and dry summer weather created further stress for potato crops.
The combination has severely affected tuber development, leaving farmers with smaller-than-usual potatoes at harvest.
Farmers Face Pressure to Meet Processing Contracts
The impact is particularly significant for growers supplying Belgium’s large potato-processing sector.
The Comijn family farms around 500 hectares of potatoes and has contracts requiring it to deliver agreed volumes to processors. With this year’s crop struggling, the family plans to draw on stocks from last year’s unusually abundant harvest to help meet some of its contractual commitments.
However, relying on existing stocks may provide only temporary relief if the smaller harvest results in a sustained reduction in available processing potatoes.
Belgium’s Global Frozen Fries Industry at Risk
The potential shortage matters well beyond Belgian farms.
Belgium is the world’s biggest exporter of frozen fries, while its potato-processing industry handles more than six million tonnes of potatoes annually. Around 90% of the frozen fries produced in Belgium are exported to more than 120 markets worldwide.
Any significant reduction in suitable processing potatoes could therefore have implications for the wider global frozen fries supply chain.
Processors require potatoes of the right size and shape to produce the long, consistent fries demanded by consumers and food-service customers. Smaller potatoes can reduce processing efficiency and may not meet the specifications required for fry production.
Fry Shops Struggle to Find the Right Potatoes
The challenges are also being noticed by Belgium’s famous fry shops.
At Maison Antoine, a well-known fry kiosk in Brussels, owner Pascal Willaert explained that large, elongated potatoes are ideal for making fries.
Pascal Willaert, owner of Maison Antoine, a renowned Brussels fry kiosk:
"But right now, with the seasons varying so wildly, it's hard to find the perfect potato for fries."
His comments highlight a growing challenge for Belgium’s traditional fry sector: it is not only the overall quantity of potatoes that matters, but also whether the harvested crop meets the size and quality requirements needed to produce the country’s signature fries.
Tighter Supplies Could Push Prices Higher
Belgium’s national association of fry vendors, which represents around 4,500 shops, has warned that tighter potato supplies could eventually push prices higher.
If farmers harvest fewer suitable potatoes, processors and fry shops could face increased competition for available supplies. Rising costs could ultimately be passed on to consumers through higher prices for fries.
For Belgium, where fries are deeply embedded in the country’s food culture and represent a major export product, the situation highlights the growing impact of extreme weather on the potato sector.
Extreme Weather Creates New Risks for Potato Farmers
This year’s difficult harvest demonstrates how rapidly changing weather conditions can affect potato production. Heavy rainfall and storms followed by extreme heat and drought can create particularly challenging growing conditions.
For farmers like Comijn, the immediate challenge is making the most of a crop that has struggled to develop.
The Comijn family’s decision to use stocks from last year’s abundant harvest could help it meet some processor commitments, but the situation illustrates the wider uncertainty facing the industry.
With potatoes significantly smaller than normal, Belgium’s position as the world’s leading frozen fries exporter could face another test. If supplies of suitable processing potatoes tighten further, the impact could eventually reach processors, fry shops and consumers around the world.

Changeable autumnal conditions are set to continue through this coming week, with spells of wetter and windier weather developing at times.
Monday will bring a short-lived burst of warmth and sunshine before temperatures drop to levels more typical for September later in the week.
A strengthening jet stream will bring deeper, low-pressure systems as the week goes on, with the potential for minor disruption towards next weekend.
Higher pressure looks set to build again for the end of the month, but prospects of a late-September heatwave remain uncertain.
Strengthening jet stream to bring windier weather
During the start to the week, the jet stream will be relatively weak and loop to the north of the UK, allowing higher pressure to develop and a warm south-westerly airflow to take hold.
Later, the jet stream will take on a more southerly path, flowing faster and straighter towards our shores. This will mean lower pressure will form, bringing rain and brisk winds at times, and temperatures will drop.
A cooling trend this week
Monday will be the warmest day of the week, with the air coming in from a south-westerly direction.
Many areas will stay fairly cloudy, with some rain around coasts and hills in the west. Despite this it will feel warm and rather humid, with temperatures climbing above 20C in many places.
Where the sun does break through, in central and southern parts of England, temperatures could reach as high as 26C.
By Thursday the winds will turn more westerly or north-westerly, bringing a fresher air mass and a cooler feel to the weather. Temperatures by this stage will reach around 14 to 16C in Scotland and Northern Ireland, and 17 to 20C in England and Wales.
Will we see out September with a heatwave?
Forecasts are showing that areas of high pressure should have more influence on the weather for the last week of September. This may mean longer dry interludes and the chance of returning to above-average daytime temperatures, but the degree of temperature rise will depend on the positioning the high pressure relative to the UK.
While long-range forecasting is fraught with uncertainty and details are subject to change, there is currently nothing to indicate that a heatwave is on the cards.
Indeed, as autumn advances and the nights become longer, high pressure overhead could lead to some rather chilly mornings.
You can keep an eye on the temperatures where you are by checking BBC Weather online and the app.

Summary
Gujarat faces very heavy rainfall as a low-pressure system moves west-northwestwards, prompting an orange alert across several vulnerable districts.
Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh may receive heavy showers with thunderstorms, strong winds and localized waterlogging under a yellow alert.
Delhi-NCR, Haryana and Chandigarh could witness heavy rain, thunderstorms and gusty winds reaching 40 kilometres per hour today.
Several southern and northeastern states may experience heavy rainfall, while strong winds and lightning pose additional weather-related risks.
Farmers should protect harvested crops, maintain field drainage and avoid outdoor activities during thunderstorms, lightning and severe weather conditions.
A strengthening monsoon system is set to bring a fresh spell of heavy rainfall across several parts of India, with Gujarat and Rajasthan emerging as the main areas of concern. According to the weather report issued by the India Meteorological Department (IMD) on Monday, September 14, a low-pressure area currently extending across southeastern Rajasthan, adjoining Gujarat and southwestern Madhya Pradesh is expected to move west-northwestwards during the next 24 hours.
The system is likely to reach southern Rajasthan and northern Gujarat, increasing rainfall activity across the region. A cyclonic circulation associated with the system extends up to about 5.8 kilometres above sea level and tilts southwestwards with height. Its influence is expected to strengthen thunderstorms and rainfall over Gujarat, Rajasthan and neighbouring areas.
Gujarat faces the most significant weather threat, with the IMD issuing an orange alert for heavy to very heavy rainfall in parts of the state. Some locations could receive between 115.6 to 204.4 millimetres of rain. Intense downpours may cause waterlogging in low-lying areas, disrupt road traffic and create temporary difficulties for commuters.
Eastern Rajasthan and western Madhya Pradesh have also been placed under a yellow alert. Several areas may record heavy rainfall between 64.5 to 115.5 millimetres, accompanied by thunderstorms and strong winds. With the low-pressure system continuing to move west-northwestwards, isolated spells of intense rain remain possible.
The weather is also expected to turn unsettled over Delhi-NCR, Haryana and Chandigarh. The IMD has forecast heavy rainfall in parts of these areas and issued a yellow alert. Thunderstorms may be accompanied by winds reaching 30 to 40 kilometres per hour.
Weather conditions may vary sharply across the National Capital Region, with some neighbourhoods receiving intense showers while nearby areas experience only light rain or cloudy skies. Lightning is also possible during thunderstorms, prompting residents to exercise caution and avoid unnecessary outdoor movement during severe weather.
A western disturbance is currently present as a trough in the middle levels of the atmosphere. Its influence could bring clouds, thunderstorms and rainfall to Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand. The interaction between the western disturbance and active monsoon conditions may also affect weather across Punjab, Haryana, Delhi and other parts of northern India.
Meanwhile, several southern and northeastern states are also likely to experience significant weather activity. Arunachal Pradesh, Assam and Meghalaya could receive heavy rain, while Kerala, Mahe, central Maharashtra, Odisha, Telangana and parts of Tamil Nadu and Puducherry may also see substantial showers.
Strong winds are another major concern. Andhra Pradesh, south interior Karnataka and Tamil Nadu may experience winds of 40 to 50 kilometres per hour. Rajasthan, Haryana, Punjab, Bihar, Jharkhand, Odisha, Telangana, West Bengal and Sikkim could see winds reaching 30 to 40 kilometres per hour.
Thunderstorms and lightning are possible in parts of Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Meghalaya, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat and Uttarakhand, increasing risks for people outdoors.
Despite widespread rainfall, temperatures remain high in some regions. Sri Ganganagar in Rajasthan recorded the country's highest maximum temperature on September 13 at 39.9 degrees Celsius. Haflong in Assam recorded the lowest minimum temperature among the plains at 17.5 degrees Celsius.
Rainfall during the previous 24 hours was significant in several cities. Hyderabad and Mumbai's Santacruz each recorded 90 millimetres, Ahmedabad received 60 millimetres, while Mokampur in Dehradun recorded 50 millimetres.
Authorities have urged residents to avoid open areas, trees and electricity poles during thunderstorms and lightning. Drivers should exercise caution and avoid waterlogged roads.
Farmers have been advised to protect harvested crops, ensure proper drainage in fields and avoid irrigation or pesticide spraying during adverse weather. Agricultural workers should stay indoors during lightning activity, while livestock should be moved to safe shelters.
With the low-pressure system expected to advance towards Gujarat and Rajasthan, the next 24 hours will remain crucial. Widespread rain, thunderstorms and strong winds are likely to keep weather conditions unsettled across several parts of the country.

Heavy rains lash Gujarat; IMD issues red alert for eight districts
Torrential rains battered several parts of Gujarat on Monday, inundating roads and underpasses and disrupting normal life, as the India Meteorological Department (IMD) issued a red alert for eight districts and forecast more heavy showers.
Central Gujarat bore the brunt of the downpour, with Borsad taluka in Anand district recording 138 mm of rain and Dholka in Ahmedabad district receiving 102 mm between 6 am and 2 pm, according to the State Emergency Operation Centre (SEOC).
Ahmedabad city recorded 84 mm during the same eight-hour period, leaving low-lying residential areas inundated and severely reducing visibility for commuters. Knee-deep water brought traffic to a halt on several major roads and created flood-like conditions in parts of the city.
Authorities have deployed 38 teams of the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) and State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) in vulnerable districts as a precautionary measure.
South Gujarat also witnessed heavy overnight rainfall, with Kaprada in Valsad district receiving 113 mm in the 24 hours ending at 6 am on Monday.
Gujarat has so far received 80.23 per cent of its seasonal average rainfall, while South Gujarat has crossed 110 per cent of its seasonal average, the SEOC said.
Officials said 35 of the state's 206 water reservoirs were on high alert, while warnings had been issued for 13 other reservoirs.
The IMD has issued a red alert for Ahmedabad, Gandhinagar, Surendranagar, Rajkot, Morbi, Porbandar, Jamnagar and Devbhumi Dwarka, forecasting heavy to very heavy rainfall in these districts.
Weather conditions are expected to improve from Tuesday, with lighter spells likely in coastal districts.

Ahmedabad has been placed under a red warning for heavy rain and thunderstorms, according to the India Meteorological Department's (IMD) nowcast issued at 10 am on September 14, 2026. The warning is valid for the next three hours.
The IMD has warned of heavy rain exceeding 15 mm per hour at isolated places in Ahmedabad, accompanied by moderate thunderstorms and surface winds reaching 41-61 kmph in gusts. The probability of cloud-to-ground lightning has been assessed at more than 60%.
19 other districts under heavy-rain warning
Along with Ahmedabad, the heavy-rain warning covers Sabarkantha, Gandhinagar, Surendranagar, Morbi, Bhavnagar, Vadodara, Anand, Kheda, Aravalli, Mehsana, Rajkot, Botad, Amreli, Junagadh, Gir Somnath, Diu, Jamnagar and Bharuch.

These include Banaskantha, Patan, Kachchh, Devbhoomi Dwarka, Porbandar, Mahisagar, Panchmahal, Dahod, Chhota Udepur, Narmada, Surat, Tapi, Dang, Navsari and Valsad, besides Daman and Dadra & Nagar Haveli.
IMD warns of waterlogging and traffic disruption
For areas experiencing heavy rain, the IMD has warned of waterlogging and flooding in low-lying areas, heavy traffic congestion, drain overflow and falling trees or advertising hoardings because of gusty winds.
The department has advised people in affected areas to restrict movement, check traffic conditions before travelling and avoid locations prone to waterlogging. Residents of vulnerable or old structures and areas near rivers and drains have also been advised to take precautions.

Heavy rain lashed the state on Ganesh Chaturthi today, 14 September. Between 6am and 10am, rainfall was recorded in 172 talukas, with Borsad in Anand receiving the highest at 4.52 inches, followed by Godhra in Panchmahal with 3.39 inches. Eight talukas recorded more than 2 inches of rain.
Heavy rain in Vadodara caused waterlogging on roads in the Raopura, Machhipith and Panigate areas. Despite the disruption caused by the rain, people remained enthusiastic about Bappa’s arrival. Several parts of Ahmedabad were also covered by dark skies amid rainfall. Meanwhile, farmers in Talala Gir are worried as heavy rain is damaging their crops.
For the first time this season, the Kalwa River in Junagadh is in spate, while water flow has also been recorded at Damodar Kund. Heavy rain is lashing the upper reaches of Datar Hill, with water flowing down the slopes like a river. A large inflow into Willingdon Dam has also raised the possibility of it overflowing.
Over the past 24 hours, rainfall ranging from 1 mm to 5.5 inches has been recorded in 240 talukas across the state. Nine talukas received more than 3 inches of rain, while 17 recorded more than 2 inches. The highest rainfall during this period was 4.45 inches in Kaprada, Valsad.
Alert for thunderstorms and strong winds in 19 districts of South Gujarat and Saurashtra
Four rain-bearing systems are active simultaneously across the state, prompting an alert for thunderstorms and strong winds. The Meteorological Department has forecast heavy rain until 1pm today, with a possibility of heavy rainfall accompanied by winds of 41 to 61 km/h and a more than 60% chance of lightning in Sabarkantha, Gandhinagar, Ahmedabad, Surendranagar, Morbi, Bhavnagar, Vadodara, Anand, Kheda, Aravalli, Mehsana, Rajkot, Botad, Amreli, Junagadh, Gir Somnath, Diu, Jamnagar and Bharuch.
Moderate rain accompanied by strong winds is likely in Banaskantha, Patan, Kutch, Devbhumi Dwarka, Porbandar, Mahisagar, Panchmahal, Dahod, Chhota Udaipur, Narmada, Surat, Tapi, Dang, Navsari, Valsad, Daman and Dadra and Nagar Haveli.
According to Meteorological Department Director A. K. Das, fishermen have been strongly advised not to venture into the sea until 15 September, as winds of 60 to 70 km/h and high waves are expected along the coast.

9 dead in Nagaland’s Tuensang civil hospital after suspected spurious liquor consumption
The incident prompted DGP Rupin Sharma to issue a red alert asking people to abstain from drinking liquor.
Dimapur, Sept 14: At least nine people were reported dead in Tuensang civil hospital in the last three days after consuming suspected spurious liquor, prompting Nagaland DGP Rupin Sharma to issue a red alert asking people to abstain from drinking liquor.
The individuals complained of breathlessness after consuming the adulterated alcohol, causing their deaths. Though the circumstances leading to the deaths are yet to be officially ascertained, DGP Sharma said the victims reportedly succumbed to what is suspected to be spurious liquor.
In a Facebook post, he said the deaths were suspected to be linked to spurious liquor, specifically suspected rum, calling them alarming. He advised the people of the state, particularly in Mon, Mokokchung, Tuensang, Longleng, Kiphire, Shamator and Noklak districts, not to consume liquor as a precautionary measure.
The DGP said preliminary findings suggested that the victims may have consumed a tainted batch of rum, even as the investigation is on to trace the source of the suspected contaminated alcohol and bring those responsible to task.
Meanwhile, authorities have urged the public to stay vigilant and immediately report any suspicious sale or distribution of liquor in their respective areas.

Performances and concerts will continue even during a yellow alert: losing a ticket or listening to air defense – the viewer's choice
The Ministry of Culture has prepared recommendations for holding concerts, festivals, performances, and other mass events during the yellow level of air attack threat. These recommendations were prepared in accordance with the resolution of the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine dated September 4, 2026, No. 1092.
The document does not provide for automatic cancellation of the event after the announcement of the yellow level, but places the obligation on the organizer to pre-determine shelters, evacuation routes, and procedures in case the situation changes. At the same time, the visitor has the right to independently decide whether to stay at the event or move to the shelter.
What action plan the organizer should develop, how long after the all-clear it is allowed to continue the event, and whether ticket refunds will be given in case of cancellation – more details in the material by the "Judicial and Legal Newspaper".
Yellow level – not yet automatic cancellation
The document applies to organizers regardless of ownership form – from state and municipal institutions to private companies and other business entities.
The establishment of the yellow threat level before the event does not mean automatic postponement or cancellation of the concert. The organizer makes the decision to start or continue the event, but several conditions must be met.
In particular, a shelter accessible to visitors, participants, and staff must be identified. The organizer must know its capacity and consider it when determining the maximum allowable number of people at the event. It is also necessary to ensure actual access to the shelter throughout the event and define the route by which people can reach it.
That is, if there are 500 people at the concert and the available shelter is designed for a significantly smaller number, the organizer cannot simply ignore this discrepancy.
Before the event starts, the organizer must assess how many people can realistically be safely accommodated, taking into account staff, performers, and other participants. Additionally, the organizer must check for any official decisions from military command, military administrations, or other authorized bodies that prohibit or restrict holding events in the relevant territory.
